stem:
A 41-year-old man with known adrenal insufficiency presents with vomiting and confusion after a febrile illness.

| Measurement | Result | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Blood pressure | 78/44 mm Hg | — |
| Glucose | 48 mg/dL | — |
| Sodium | 124 mEq/L | — |

Which immediate treatment is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: IV hydrocortisone plus saline and dextrose
options.misconception: None; this replaces cortisol while correcting volume and glucose deficits.
options.explanation: Suspected adrenal crisis requires immediate parenteral glucocorticoid therapy with aggressive isotonic fluid and glucose support.

options.label: B
options.text: IV insulin plus dextrose and observation
options.misconception: Insulin-dextrose may temporarily shift potassium but does not treat cortisol deficiency or shock.
options.explanation: The full syndrome is adrenal crisis, so endocrine replacement and volume resuscitation cannot be delayed.

options.label: C
options.text: Oral prednisone after an ACTH stimulation test
options.misconception: Diagnostic confirmation is being prioritized over treatment of a life-threatening emergency.
options.explanation: Treatment should begin immediately when adrenal crisis is suspected; vomiting also makes oral therapy unreliable.

options.label: D
options.misconception: Myxedema coma is being confused with an adrenal crisis in a patient with known adrenal insufficiency.
options.explanation: Hypotonic fluid would not address shock, and thyroid hormone does not replace the missing glucocorticoid.

options.label: E
options.misconception: Chronic mineralocorticoid replacement is being substituted for emergency resuscitation.
options.explanation: An unstable, vomiting patient needs IV therapy; fluid restriction would worsen severe volume depletion.

context: Learning objective: treat adrenal crisis before waiting for confirmatory testing. The immediate priorities are parenteral glucocorticoid replacement, isotonic volume resuscitation, and dextrose when hypoglycemia is present.
